cucumber

Write specifications in plain-language Gherkin, run them from R as testthat tests, and read the results in the console or in Cucumber’s own HTML report. An R implementation of the Cucumber testing framework.

Installation 

install.packages("cucumber")

Where to start

  • New to cucumber? Get started: write and run your first feature.
  • New to BDD? Read Behavior-Driven Development.
  • Know testthat? See cucumber and testthat.
  • Looking something up? Open the function reference or the Gherkin reference.

Run your first feature

A feature file describes behavior in Gherkin

Feature: Addition
  Scenario: Adding 2 integers
    When I add 1 and 1
    Then the result is 2
  Scenario: Adding integer and float
    When I add 1 and 1.1
    Then the result is 2.1
  Scenario: Adding float and float
    When I add 1.1 and 1.1
    Then the result is 2.2

and step definitions run each step in R

when("I add {float} and {float}", function(x, y, context) {
  context$result <- x + y
})

then("the result is {float}", function(expected, context) {
  expect_equal(context$result, expected)
})

Each Feature is a testthat context and each Scenario a testthat::test_that() case, so you get feedback on each Scenario separately. Run them with cucumber::test():

withr::with_dir(pass_dir, {
  cucumber::test(filter = "addition")
})
  |  F  P  U  S  OK | Feature
v |               3 | Addition

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
  3 scenarios (3 passed)
  6 steps (6 passed)
  0m00.100s (executing steps: 0m00.100s)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When a step fails, the reporter shows which step broke and why, and where its definition is. Get started walks through a failure, the other console reporters and where to put the files.

Reports

Write the official Cucumber HTML report of a run with CucumberHtmlReporter, and its JUnit XML report with CucumberJunitReporter. Steps and hooks attach screenshots and logs to it, like those of a failing shinytest2 scenario: see the Reports article and its report.

Scenarios as documentation

Feature files already say how your package behaves, so let them document it. Tag the scenarios that illustrate a function with @rd

Feature: Basket
  A basket holds the items a customer wants to buy.

  @rd
  Scenario: Add an item
    Given an empty basket
    When I add 1 item
    Then the basket has 1 item

  Scenario: Remove an item from an empty basket
    Given an empty basket
    When I remove 1 item
    Then the basket is empty

and put them in its help page with features_rd():

#' Add items to a basket
#' @eval cucumber::features_rd(features = "basket.feature")
#' @export
add <- function(basket, n) basket + n

devtools::document() adds a Behavior section to ?add with the feature’s description and the tagged scenarios:

Add items to a basket

Description:

     Add items to a basket

Usage:

     add(basket, n)
     
Behavior:

     Feature: Basket
       A basket holds the items a customer wants to buy.
     
       Scenario: Add an item
         Given an empty basket
         When I add 1 item
         Then the basket has 1 item
     
     Source: 'tests/acceptance/basket.feature'

The help pages of this package are written this way, see ?hook or ?test: the scenarios that test cucumber explain it, and stay true because they run.

How steps are matched, and the parameter types you can use, are in How it works.
